source: Fleck & Weisberg (2004) The use of verbal protocols as data: an analysis of insight in the candle problem
finding: Thinking aloud did not change candle-problem solving. So protocols can be used as data on insight, and verbal overshadowing did not show up.
numbers: N=58 students. Box solution: 8 of 34 verbalizers (23.5%) vs 5 of 18 silent (27.7%), chi2(1,N=52)=0.113, p=.736. Box-solver time 5.97 vs 5.32 min, t(11)=0.351, p=.732, d=.21. Overall 25% solved (n=13), mean 5.72 min.
limits: Single problem, 10 min limit, undergraduates. Silent group smaller. Coding by two raters (agreement 90-93%).
agent_relevance: Writing out reasoning does not by itself harm hard-insight solving in humans, so a visible chain of thought is a fair scaffold step. Supports the ordinary-process view.

source: Fleck & Weisberg (2004) candle problem, impasse analysis
finding: Restructuring was common, but impasse was not needed for the insight solution. Those who hit an impasse were LESS likely to find the box solution. This goes against the classic stuck-then-flash sequence.
numbers: Of 34 protocols, 44% (15) showed some impasse; 1 of 15 (7%) with impasse found the box solution vs 7 of 19 (37%) without. chi2(1,N=34)=4.242, p=.039, phi=.35. None of 3 with true impasse (full stop) solved. About 75% of first solutions were not the box.
limits: Small n. 10 min may be too short for impasse breakout (authors say so). Impasse criteria were widened by the authors.
agent_relevance: Being stuck is not a sign that a flash will come. Do not wait for a stall; change the problem representation by gradual modification of failed attempts (an operator, not a pause).

source: Fleck & Weisberg (2004) discussion of verbal overshadowing replication failures
finding: The authors argue Schooler et al. (1993) overshadowing on insight problems may rest on instructions and a non-insight training problem, and that the wider verbal-overshadowing effect has failed to replicate in several labs.
numbers: No new numbers. Cites Meissner et al. 2001 failures; Meissner & Brigham found effect mainly for extended description of visual stimuli.
limits: Argument from the authors, who favour the ordinary-process view.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: verbalizing hurts only some tasks (perceptual, extended descriptions). For text-based reasoning, explicit steps are not shown to damage creativity.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) Does incubation enhance problem solving? A meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin 135(1)
finding: A real but small incubation benefit. Weighted mean effect is small to moderate; most of the 117 studies are positive; no sign of publication bias by funnel regression.
numbers: 117 studies, 3,606 participants, median n=25 per study. 85 studies positive. Unweighted mean d=0.41 (SD 0.71), adjusted 0.36 (CI 0.26-0.45). Weighted random-effects mean d=0.29 (CI 0.21-0.39). Q=173.99, df=113, p<.001. Between-study variance .0834. Funnel regression beta=.08, p=.41.
limits: Heterogeneous designs; many tiny samples; includes unpublished work. Effects depend on moderators (see b05).
agent_relevance: Incubation (set aside, return) helps modestly. An agent can emulate it with a fresh restart or a different-task gap between attempts, but expect gains near d=0.3, not large.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009) moderators
finding: Divergent-thinking tasks gain more from incubation than linguistic or visual insight tasks. Longer preparation gives larger effects. A demanding task during the break shrinks the effect. For linguistic insight problems a low-demand task beat plain rest.
numbers: Moderators tested by weighted least squares: problem type, misleading or relevant cues, preparation length, incubation length, load of the interpolated task. Per-subgroup numbers are in their Table 4 (not extracted here).
limits: Subgroup sizes uneven; creative-problem and unoccupied-rest subgroups had too few studies for regression.
agent_relevance: Supports two kinds of incubation: knowledge-based (divergent) vs strategic (insight). For the agent: use restart/gap mainly for idea generation; give a long prepare phase first; do not fill the gap with heavy work.

source: Nieuwenstein, Wierenga, Morey et al. (2015) On making the right choice: meta-analysis and large-scale replication of the unconscious thought advantage. JDM
finding: Unconscious thought (distraction before choosing) gives no reliable advantage over deliberation. The apparent small effect vanishes after correcting for publication bias, and a large replication found nothing.
numbers: Meta-analysis: 61 effect sizes, N 40-399 per study. Random-effects Hedges g=0.15 (CI 0.03-0.26, p=.01); after trim-and-fill g=0.018 (CI -0.10 to 0.14). Funnel asymmetry p=.04. Replication N=399: correct choice 58.2% deliberation vs 61.9% distraction, n.s.; Bayes factor 7.83 for the null.
quote: there exists no reliable support for the claim that a momentary diversion of thought leads to better decision making than a period of deliberation
limits: Choice tasks (multi-attribute), not creative idea generation. Does not test incubation in insight problems.
agent_relevance: Failed replication of the strongest implicit-processing claim. Do not design the agent around a hidden 'unconscious' stage that is trusted without a check.

source: Stuyck, Cleeremans & Van den Bussche (2022) Aha! under pressure: the Aha! experience is not constrained by cognitive load. Cognition
finding: Dual-task test of a key prediction. Under working-memory load, analytic (non-insight) solutions dropped and slowed, while insight solutions stayed mostly unaffected. Insight solutions were also more often correct and more confident.
numbers: N=106, 70 compound remote associate puzzles, no/low/high digit load. Insight vs non-insight accuracy about 94% vs 77% in one analysis, d=-1.57. Insight more frequent than non-insight (M 16.4 vs 10.5, d about 0.5-0.9 across load levels); non-insight solutions fell with load (M 15.8 to 7.9, d=0.66).
limits: Verbal remote-associate puzzles only; self-report classification of insight; load is digit memory.
agent_relevance: Discriminating experiment: it favours a distinct, load-free (implicit-like) route for insight, against pure ordinary-process theory. Suggests two routes in the scaffold: effortful stepwise search plus a cheap associative route that needs no working space.

source: Stuyck, Aben, Cleeremans & Van den Bussche (2021) The Aha! moment: is insight a different form of problem solving? Consciousness and Cognition
finding: Tests Weisberg's integrated theory. Impasse was NOT required for insight. Restructuring came before insight more often but also occurred in non-insight solutions. People could report on the solution search, which supports conscious operations. The usual insight accuracy and speed advantage did not appear here.
numbers: N=42, 70 compound remote associate puzzles, self-ratings of difficulty, confidence, suddenness, impasse, restructuring. Insight higher in suddenness and confidence; accuracy and speed advantage not replicated.
limits: Abstract read only (full text not opened). Self-report measures.
agent_relevance: Two-way support: insight can be reached with conscious steps (ordinary), yet restructuring is not specific to insight. Restructuring should be an available operator at any time, not only after a stall.

source: Helie & Sun (2010) Incubation, insight, and creative problem solving: a unified theory and a connectionist model. Psychological Review 117(3)
finding: Explicit-implicit interaction (EII) theory, built in the CLARION architecture. Explicit rule-based and implicit associative processing run together, hold redundant knowledge, and their results are integrated iteratively. Simulates human data on incubation and insight.
numbers: Five principles listed in the abstract. Simulations reproduce human insight and incubation data (details not read).
limits: Only the PubMed abstract was read. Model fit to selected human data; no independent test shown here. Not the model-fit numbers.
agent_relevance: Gives a blueprint: run a fast associative generator and a slow rule-based checker in parallel, then integrate. Close to our generate-then-check split.

source: Gabora (2017) Honing theory: a complex systems framework for creativity. Nonlinear Dynamics, Psychology & Life Sciences 21(1)
finding: Creativity as honing: an idea in a state of potentiality (a merged blend of many sources) is reshaped by contexts until it settles. Not a search over discrete candidates. Midway through analogy solving, answers looked like a merge of several sources.
numbers: Gabora & Saab (2011) interrupted Gick-Holyoak radiation analogy solvers: judge-coded 'honing' responses were significantly more frequent than 'structure-mapping' responses (counts not given in the review). Art students identified creators of unseen works above chance; authenticity ratings correlated across viewers (r values not given).
limits: Review paper; the key studies are small, judged by naive raters, and by the theory's own lab. Not independently replicated here.
agent_relevance: Suggests a blend step before selection: keep a mixed draft and refine it under different framings. Treat as a [S] single-lab idea.

source: Gabora (2019) Reframing convergent and divergent thought for the 21st century. CogSci
finding: Argues divergent and convergent thinking are better described as associative versus analytic modes, both used throughout, rather than two separate stages. Links to dual-process theory.
numbers: No new data.
limits: Conceptual paper.
agent_relevance: Argues against a rigid 'diverge then converge' pipeline. Let both modes switch at any state.

source: Smith, Ward & Finke (1995) Paradoxes, principles and prospects for the future of creative cognition (concluding chapter)
finding: Names the special-vs-ordinary paradox. Processes like insight, incubation and activation of disparate elements also show up in non-creative tasks. Verbalization hurts insight problems but also hurts face recognition, so it is not unique to creativity.
numbers: No new data.
limits: Secondary chapter, 1995; before the later empirical tests.
agent_relevance: Frames the question: can ordinary operators explain it? Supports using general operators for creativity tasks.

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) Japanese children's riddles as a benchmark for machine insight and metacognition (NazoNazo)
finding: Insight-style riddles are hard for LLMs. Reasoning models do better than non-reasoning ones but stay far below humans. Models often produced the right candidate but did not endorse it (verification failure).
numbers: 38 LLMs, 201 riddles, 120-item human comparison, human pilot n=126. Humans about 53% (52.9%). Non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6%. Reasoning vs non-reasoning: Welch t(24.1)=2.98, p=.0066, diff 9.8 points, d=0.946. Parameter size vs accuracy r=-0.017 (n=38); release date rho=0.402, p=.012.
limits: Japanese-language riddles; riddle scoring needs manual gold-answer checks; human subset differs from the full set.
agent_relevance: The gap is in recognizing the right answer, not producing it. Strengthens the rule that a program-side check, not the model's own feeling, accepts an answer.

source: d'Aliberti & Ribeiro (2026) The illusion of insight in reasoning models
finding: Spontaneous 'Aha' mid-trace shifts in RL-trained reasoning models are rare and mostly hurt accuracy. They do not grow with training and signal unstable inference, not self-correction. But a shift triggered from outside when entropy is high does help.
numbers: Over 1M reasoning traces. Shifts in about 6.31% of traces (7.6% for Qwen2.5-1.5B). Accuracy 2.57% for shifted vs 16.44% for non-shifted traces (N=723,200). DeepSeek-R1 shift rate 0.40-0.60%, GPT-4o 2.20-3.00% on MATH-500. Externally triggered reconsideration at high entropy: +8.41 points on MATH-500, smaller gains on crosswords and Rush Hour.
limits: Small GRPO-tuned models for training analysis; MATH-500, crosswords, Rush Hour; shifts detected by cue words and rubric LLM.
agent_relevance: Strong support for program-triggered variation: restart or reframe by code when uncertainty is high, rather than trusting the model's own 'wait, actually'.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: the open-ended homogeneity of language models
finding: LLMs repeat themselves and also converge across models on open-ended prompts. Higher temperature or min-p does not remove it.
numbers: 26,070 open-ended queries (INFINITY-CHAT), 25 models x 50 responses in a main plot; 42 models in a similarity analysis, mean within-prompt similarity 0.821. At top-p 0.9, temperature 1.0 mean pairwise similarity typically above 0.8. Under min-p, 81% of pairs still above 0.7 and 61.2% above 0.8. Cross-model similarity 71% to 82% (DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82). 31,250 human annotations.
limits: Embedding cosine similarity as the proxy for sameness; prompts are real-user chat queries.
agent_relevance: Raw sampling gives little real variety. Engineered variation (distinct framings, operators, personas, constraints) is needed. Supports our variation operators.

source: Peeperkorn, Kouwenhoven, Brown & Jordanous (2024) Is temperature the creativity parameter of large language models?
finding: Temperature is only weakly linked to novelty, moderately linked to incoherence, and unrelated to cohesion or typicality. Not a creativity dial.
numbers: Llama 2-Chat stories with human raters. Mixed-model temperature coefficient: novelty 0.308 (SE .138), coherence effect 0.240 (SE .122, higher temp = less coherent). Perplexity vs novelty 0.730 (SE .273). Exact N of stories not recorded.
limits: One model, one story task, simple stories, non-expert judges with moderate agreement.
agent_relevance: Random noise is a poor variation source. Controlled variation by operators beats raising temperature.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi & Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models
finding: Older GPT-3 models fall for intuitive traps (CRT, semantic illusions) at human-like rates; ChatGPT and GPT-4 avoid them, helped by chain of thought. Chain of thought is the 'explicit' route and it works in models.
numbers: CRT: humans 41% correct in original, LLM 38%. GPT-3-davinci-003 intuitive answers 80%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, GPT-4 0%; correct 5% (davinci) vs 59% (ChatGPT-3.5) vs 96% (GPT-4), humans 38%. Prompting chain of thought raised davinci correct from 5% to 28% (intuitive 80% to 29%). Blocking CoT: ChatGPT-4 correct 95% to 88%. Few-shot examples raised accuracy from 2% to 92% after two examples.
limits: CRT-style tasks with a known right answer, not creative production; models differ and may have seen CRT items.
agent_relevance: The explicit route can be switched on by scaffold. For modern models the implicit trap response is mostly gone on classic tasks, so novelty must come from elsewhere.

source: Weisberg (2015) Toward an integrated theory of insight in problem solving. Thinking & Reasoning 21(1)
finding: Theory that insight mainly rests on conscious analytic operations with restructuring as the special feature; unconscious processes matter only after an impasse. Described via secondary summary (Stuyck et al. 2021).
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not read; only secondary description.
agent_relevance: Background for the ordinary-process position the subfield is named for.

source: Fleck & Weisberg (2013) Insight versus analysis: evidence for diverse methods in problem solving. J. Cognitive Psychology
finding: Verbal protocols on five insight problems; conclusion that insight and analysis are two ends of a set of methods, not a sharp split. Seen only in a search snippet.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Not read. Numbers unknown.
agent_relevance: Weak support for one toolbox of methods. Need the full text before use.

source: Alogna et al. (2014) Registered replication report: Schooler & Engstler-Schooler (1990) verbal overshadowing. Perspectives on Psychological Science
finding: Registered multi-lab replication confirmed verbal overshadowing for face recognition (confirmed in Mickes & Wixted 2015 abstract). Effect size not read.
numbers: Not extracted.
limits: Face recognition lineup, not insight problems. Mickes & Wixted note the false ID rate is unknown.
agent_relevance: Boundary: overshadowing is real in perception tasks, so the failure to see it in the candle problem (b01) is task specific.

source: Mickes & Wixted (2015) On the applied implications of the verbal overshadowing effect
finding: Says the first Registered Replication Report in the journal confirmed verbal overshadowing, but it is unclear if it is memory loss or more conservative responding.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Commentary; abstract only.
agent_relevance: Shows how a famous 'explicit hurts implicit' effect can survive replication yet stay narrow.

source: Stuyck et al. (2022) design rationale: dual-process link
finding: Notes that mapping insight to Type 1 and non-insight to Type 2 is not widely held, even though Type 1 is load-free and Type 2 depends on working memory. Their load result is the test of that mapping.
numbers: See b07.
limits: Introduction text.
agent_relevance: Our two-route design should not claim a clean System 1 / System 2 split; test it.

source: Hagendorff et al. (2023), example effect
finding: Blocking chain of thought in ChatGPT-3.5 left correct answers unchanged, while in GPT-4 it caused a small drop, showing the strongest models can run the 'explicit' answer without writing it out.
numbers: ChatGPT-3.5 correct change 4 points, n.s. (p=.49). ChatGPT-4 intuitive responses 0% to 10%; correct 95% to 88%. Chain-of-thought responses fell from 97% to 0% (ChatGPT-3.5) and 84% to 0% (GPT-4).
limits: Small task set; instruction-based blocking of CoT.
agent_relevance: Written steps are not the whole of how models compute; do not treat the trace as the real process (G on trace honesty).

source: Mizumoto et al. (2025) NazoNazo, cross-language finding
finding: Thinking in Japanese did not make models better at Japanese insight riddles. Some models reasoned in English for Japanese items, others in Japanese.
numbers: Examples of thought-log language: Claude-opus-4 Japanese 21.9% vs English 78.1% of logs; Grok-4 Japanese 57.2%. Overall correctness listed per model (e.g. Grok-4 37.6%, Claude-opus-4 30.3%).
limits: Few models examined for language-of-thought.
agent_relevance: Language of reasoning is not the bottleneck; representation change is.

source: d'Aliberti & Ribeiro (2026), design of the intervention
finding: The gain from forced reconsideration is gated by entropy: top 20% highest-entropy items versus bottom 80%.
numbers: Entropy gate top 20% within domain; gains largest in that bucket; +8.41 points MATH-500 overall effect.
limits: Per-bucket numbers not extracted here.
agent_relevance: A cheap program rule: re-ask only when the model is uncertain. Matches our counted-step, code-decides principle.

source: Sio & Ormerod (2009), incubation theories
finding: Frames the rival accounts: unconscious spreading activation (special process) versus conscious search with fresh restart (ordinary process). Predicts the low-demand-task advantage would come from either selective forgetting or covert work.
numbers: See b04.
limits: Meta-analysis cannot separate the two accounts.
agent_relevance: Both accounts agree on one scaffold action: break fixation by a gap and restart, so that is the safe operator.
